newsitem.title: INDIA: Sombre India ritual to mark worst mid-air disaster.
newsitem.headline: Sombre India ritual to mark worst mid-air disaster.

text.p: India prepared a sombre ritual farewell on Thursday for victims of the world's worst mid-air collision, which killed some 350 people.

Experts said the cause of the crash could be determined inside two weeks following Wednesday's recovery of the black boxes from the wreckage of the two planes. "We will perform the last rites of the victims who are too badly burned to be identified, with the permission of their relatives," Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim told reporters.
Indian authorities said they had handed over to relatives 70 identifiable bodies of more than 250 found so far. Another 60 were too badly mutilated to be identifed.

There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 that had just taken off from New Delhi on Tuesday evening or among the 37 people on a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter that was preparing to land.
Scores of distraught relatives thronged the general hospital at Charkhi Dadri, 80 kms (50 miles) west of Delhi in bordering Haryana state, hoping against hope to identify their loved ones.
The blazing wreckage of the two aircraft, which witnesses said plummetted to earth like "fireballs", fell 10 kilometres (six miles) apart on the north Indian plain around Charkhi Dadri.
The wreckage of the Saudi plane was still smoking at dusk as searchers probed it for up to 60 more bodies they estimated still remained under the debris.
The rescue teams worked through Tuesday night and Wednesday to pull the charred and mangled bodies free of the wreckage. Shops and businesses were closed in mourning in Charkhi Dadri on Wednesday.
Residents said they were sure the pilot of the jumbo averted an even worse disaster by steering his blazing aircraft away from their villages into nearby cotton and mustard fields.
Parveen Kumar of Charkhi Dadri town, which has a population of 50,000, told Reuters: "The plane turned into a fireball, and separated into three fireballs and fell into Dadri.
"I think the pilot deliberately went over the town and tried to land in the fields."

Ibrahim said 200 wooden coffins had been prepared for the remains. The authorities had arranged to embalm bodies destined for far-off places like the northern city of Srinagar or the southern state of Kerala, before sending them home, he said.

Aviation experts said it could take less than two weeks to ascertain the cause of the collision after searchers recovered the so-called "black boxes", or flight data and cockpit voice recorders, from the wreckage on Wednesday.

"I would imagine that you would begin to have some information in less than two weeks," Stuart Matthews, chairman of the U.S.-based Flight Safety Foundation, told Reuters on the sidelines of an international aviation safety meet in Dubai.
Speculation on the cause had ranged from inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of instructions from ground controllers.

Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant at India's Civil Aviation Ministry, ruled out both. He said the transcript of the final conversations between the pilots and ground control showed both understood their instructions.
Speculation that ageing equipment at Delhi airport might be to blame was "absolutely incorrect", he told a news conference.
A new $92 million state-of-the-art air traffic control system being built by U.S. firm Raytheon for Bombay and Delhi airports would be operational by early next year, he added.

Chandra refused comment on other possible causes raised by experts, including speculation the pilot of the KazAir plane could have misconverted the altitude instructions he was given in feet, the international norm, rather than metres.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told reporters, "We will not spare any culprit." His government would implement all the recommendations made by High Court judge R.C. Lahoti, who has been appointed to conduct an inquiry, he added.
The U.S. State Department said three Americans were aboard a Saudi Arabia Airlines plane that collided with another jet over India, killing 349 people.
Deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said two of the Americans were passengers and one was a crew member on the Saudi Boeing 747.

A Saudi newspaper said the victims included 215 Indians, 13 Saudis, and three Pakistanis. Nepal's Foreign Ministry said there were 53 Nepalis on board, most of them headed for jobs as manual labourers, drivers and plumbers.
There were three women,two American and one British, aboard.

The KazAir plane was carrying 25 businessmen who had chartered it to fly empty to Delhi, where they planned to buy $1.5 million worth of woollens for sale at home, KazAir Delhi airport manager Rajiv Bhaskar said.
Bhaskar said there were also two children and 10 crew on the plane, which broke in two. All 37 bodies were recovered.
